source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-based reasoning: foundational issues, methodological variations, and system approaches. AI Communications 7(1):39-59
finding: Defines the 4R cycle: Retrieve the most similar case(s), Reuse their information to solve the problem, Revise the proposed solution, Retain the useful parts of the experience. The paper gives it as a general cycle, not a tested model.
numbers: Stated as a numbered list and a figure (new case -> retrieve -> retrieved case -> reuse -> solved case -> revise -> confirmed case -> retain -> case base). No experiments in the paper.
quote: As a mnemonic, try 'the four REs'
limits: A survey and framework paper. It reports no measurements of its own. The cycle describes existing systems (CHEF, CASEY, PROTOS, CREEK); it was not a tested result.
agent_relevance: Our schema already has retrieve-like (S0, S2), generate, test and revise (S5) states. The 4R cycle adds retain, which a single-run schema lacks. Retain only matters across tasks.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-based reasoning: foundational issues, methodological variations, and system approaches. AI Communications 7(1):39-59
finding: Frames CBR as problem solving plus learning: learning is a by-product of solving. Success is retained; on failure the reason is identified and remembered to avoid the same mistake.
numbers: Sec 1.3: CBR is 'regarded a subfield of machine learning'; the case base is updated 'no matter how the problem was solved'.
quote: Learning in CBR occurs as a natural by-product of problem solving.
limits: Conceptual claim. The paper later admits effective learning needs well-worked methods to extract relevant knowledge and index it.
agent_relevance: Retain is cheap to start but needs rules for what to keep. Store failures with their cause, not only successes.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-based reasoning: foundational issues, methodological variations, and system approaches. AI Communications 7(1):39-59
finding: Grounds CBR in psychology with a few citations: Ross 1989 (role of specific past situations), Schank 1982 (dynamic memory), Anderson 1983 (people use past cases as models early in learning), Rouse via Kolodner 1985 (experts rely on past cases), Gentner and Carbonell on analogy.
numbers: Plausibility argument only. No effect sizes are given for any of these human studies.
limits: The human evidence is cited, not reviewed. The behavioural studies (Ross 1984, Gick & Holyoak 1980, Anderson 1983) must be read in later angles.
agent_relevance: Do not treat the 4R cycle as proven human cognition. It is an engineering framework with a psychological motivation.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-based reasoning: foundational issues, methodological variations, and system approaches. AI Communications 7(1):39-59
finding: Separates CBR from nearby methods: instance-based (feature vector plus class), memory-based (large memory, parallel search), analogy-based (cross-domain mapping). A typical case is rich and structured, and the system adapts the retrieved solution using background knowledge.
numbers: Sec 2. CBR is called 'a form of intra-domain analogy'; analogy research focuses on cross-domain mapping.
limits: Boundaries are soft; the authors say a system labelled with another approach can still be typical CBR.
agent_relevance: Our reuse is intra-domain (same benchmark family), the cheaper and better-supported end of the range.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-based reasoning: foundational issues, methodological variations, and system approaches. AI Communications 7(1):39-59
finding: Gives a task-method decomposition. Retrieve = identify features, initially match, search, select. Reuse = copy, adapt. Revise = evaluate solution, repair fault. Retain = extract, index, integrate. The partitions are claimed complete at that level.
numbers: Fig 2 task hierarchy. Task partitions are complete, method sets incomplete. The figure gives no control structure over subtasks.
limits: Knowledge-level modelling (Components of Expertise, Steels). Control is left to the problem-solving method, so the model does not say when to skip a step.
agent_relevance: Each sub-task is a slot a model can fill while code does control. Fits our rule that the program decides transitions.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-based reasoning: foundational issues, methodological variations, and system approaches. AI Communications 7(1):39-59
finding: Two classic memory models. Schank/Kolodner dynamic memory: a discrimination network of generalized episodes (norms) with indices; a case is pushed down the network; shared parts of two cases become a new generalized episode. Bareiss/Porter PROTOS: categories, exemplars ranked by prototypicality, with feature, case and difference links.
numbers: Retrieval in dynamic memory finds the generalized episode with most norms in common, then follows indices for extra features. Index count can grow explosively; CYRUS allows only a small index vocabulary.
limits: Described as simplified models of human memory. A footnote says 'most features in common' may not be the right similarity criterion.
agent_relevance: Memory structure decides retrieval quality. For an LLM the 'index' is the text used for lookup, so choose it on purpose.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-based reasoning: foundational issues, methodological variations, and system approaches. AI Communications 7(1):39-59
finding: Retrieval: knowledge-poor (surface similarity, e.g. CYRUS, PATDEX-1) versus knowledge-intensive (explanation-based, e.g. PROTOS, CASEY, CREEK). Matching is two-stage: a cheap candidate set, then a costlier select that builds explanations and expectations.
numbers: Candidates come from direct index pointers, a searched index structure, or a domain model. A relevance test may check that the retrieved solution type fits the new problem.
limits: Surface similarity wins where domain knowledge is hard to get; knowledge-intensive wins where it exists. No head-to-head numbers.
agent_relevance: Cheap recall followed by a costly fit check matches current retrieve-then-rerank practice.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-based reasoning: foundational issues, methodological variations, and system approaches. AI Communications 7(1):39-59
finding: Reuse has two forms. Transformational reuse applies operators to the old solution. Derivational reuse replays the old method (operators, subgoals, failed paths) in the new context; successful paths are tried first and failed ones avoided.
numbers: Examples: CASEY (transformational, rules indexed by differences); Analogy/Prodigy (derivational, falls back to means-ends planning if replay fails).
limits: Transformational reuse needs a strong operator model. Derivational reuse needs the old reasoning trace stored.
agent_relevance: Derivational reuse means storing the path, not only the answer. Our G10 says reasoning text is not evidence, so store paths with their checked outcome and treat them as hints.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-based reasoning: foundational issues, methodological variations, and system approaches. AI Communications 7(1):39-59
finding: Revise has two tasks: evaluate (apply to the real world, ask a teacher, or run a simulation) and repair (explain the failure, then modify). Evaluation is usually outside the CBR system. Unevaluated cases may be stored but must be marked non-evaluated.
numbers: CHEF runs a recipe on an internal causal model, explains goal failures, and learns failure situations by explanation-based learning so later plans anticipate them. In medicine, outcome can take hours to months.
limits: Revise needs a trustworthy evaluator. CHEF's evaluator was an internal model, which works only where such a model exists.
agent_relevance: Matches G2 and G3: revise only from real output. A stored case must carry whether it was verified. Do not retrieve unverified cases as proof.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-based reasoning: foundational issues, methodological variations, and system approaches. AI Communications 7(1):39-59
finding: Retain has three parts: extract (problem, solution, justification, method trace, failures), index (the central indexing problem), integrate (adjust index strengths by success or failure; PATDEX updates a relevance matrix with a connectionist rule).
numbers: Failures can be kept as separate failure cases, to give a reminding at the next similar failure. Trivial indexing uses all input features. The learned case can be tested by re-entering the original problem.
quote: The 'indexing problem' is a central and much focused problem in case-based reasoning.
limits: Indexing is called a knowledge acquisition problem and is left unsolved. No policy for what to drop is given; that came later (utility problem).
agent_relevance: Keep failure cases with their cause, re-run the stored problem as a retention test, and weight retrieval by past success.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-based reasoning: foundational issues, methodological variations, and system approaches. AI Communications 7(1):39-59
finding: Integrated approaches: CASEY falls back on a slow causal model and stores the result as a new case, so CBR is speed-up learning. BOLERO uses a case-based planner as meta-level control over a rule base.
numbers: CASEY: when the case-based method fails, the model-based method solves it and the answer is retained. BOLERO: the meta-level re-plans whenever new information arrives.
limits: Speed-up is design intent; this survey gives no timing data.
agent_relevance: Cases as a shortcut for a slow solver fit: use stored cases to skip search, and fall back to the full method when no case passes the relevance test.

source: Lopez de Mantaras et al. (2005) Retrieval, reuse, revision and retention in case-based reasoning. Knowledge Engineering Review 20(3):215-240
finding: Traces CBR roots in cognitive science: story understanding (Schank & Abelson 1977), then dynamic memory theory with Memory Organization Packets that give remindings (Schank 1982). Remindings can cross contexts. When expectations fail, prior explanations are recalled (SWALE).
numbers: SWALE uses MOP-based expectations until it meets an anomaly, then retrieves prior explanations and adapts them.
limits: Theory- and model-driven. Human data are not tabulated.
agent_relevance: Anomaly-triggered retrieval (recall a past explanation only when expectations fail) matches our rule to act on a signal, not a schedule (G1).

source: Lopez de Mantaras et al. (2005) Retrieval, reuse, revision and retention in case-based reasoning. Knowledge Engineering Review 20(3):215-240
finding: Retrieval moved from raw similarity to utility. Bergmann et al. 2001 call similarity a proxy for solution utility. Smyth & Keane (1994-1998) argue the most similar case may be impossible to adapt; adaptation-guided retrieval scores adaptability during retrieval and is reported to cut adaptation failures and cost.
numbers: Direction of effect only; the original Smyth & Keane numbers were not opened.
quote: Effective retrieval is not simply a matter of finding cases that are similar but cases that are usefully similar.
limits: Described by the review, not the original experiments.
agent_relevance: Rank retrieved cases by whether they can be applied, not by embedding closeness. A near case that cannot be adapted is worse than a farther one that can.

source: Lopez de Mantaras et al. (2005) Retrieval, reuse, revision and retention in case-based reasoning. Knowledge Engineering Review 20(3):215-240
finding: The utility problem hits case learning. As the case base grows, mean retrieval time rises while adaptation savings per new case shrink. Past a critical size, adding cases lowers overall efficiency.
numbers: Smyth & Cunningham (1996) argue this is inevitable under general assumptions. The idea comes from Minton (1990) on speed-up rules in explanation-based learning.
quote: Eventually the increase in retrieval time as a result of a new case addition is greater than the adaptation savings offered.
limits: Taken from the review, not the original papers. In LLM agents the retrieval cost shows up as context length and noise.
agent_relevance: Do not retain everything. Memento's K sweep (an LLM result) shows the same flat shape after a few cases.

source: Lopez de Mantaras et al. (2005) Retrieval, reuse, revision and retention in case-based reasoning. Knowledge Engineering Review 20(3):215-240
finding: Remedies for harmful and redundant cases. Condensed NN (Hart 1968) removes redundancy; Wilson's edited NN (1972) removes noise. Smyth & Keane 1995 use a competence model to rank cases by problem-solving coverage and delete the least critical first. Competence-guided addition and footprint retrieval followed.
numbers: Footprint retrieval: stage one finds the most similar footprint case (a covering set of the case base); stage two searches cases near it.
limits: Competence models need a notion of which problems a case solves. That is easy in classification and hard in open-ended tasks.
agent_relevance: Selective retention: keep cases that cover distinct problem types, drop near-duplicates, and test whether a retained case ever helped a later task.

source: Lopez de Mantaras et al. (2005) Retrieval, reuse, revision and retention in case-based reasoning. Knowledge Engineering Review 20(3):215-240
finding: Case-base maintenance grew out of the utility problem. Wilson & Leake (2001) split maintenance policy into data gathering, triggering (periodic, conditional, ad hoc) and operations. Leake & Wilson (1999) warn that in changing environments the problem-solution regularity assumption must be checked and the case base corrected.
numbers: Retention is described as inseparable from maintenance of the other knowledge containers: vocabulary, similarity, adaptation.
limits: The authors treat maintenance as a broader view of retain. Few quantitative comparisons are given.
agent_relevance: Retain needs a drift check. If tasks change, old cases can mislead. Stamp each case with date, model version and verification state.

source: Aha, Kibler & Albert (1991) Instance-based learning algorithms. Machine Learning 6:37-66
finding: IB1 (store every instance, classify by nearest neighbour) is proven to learn a broad class of concepts. IB2 stores only instances it misclassified; this cuts storage a lot but is sensitive to noise. IB3 adds a significance test that accepts or drops instances by their classification record, and fixes the noise problem.
limits: On the artificial 2-D domain at 10% noise IB3 used 5.8% of instances for classification, IB2 28.2%, IB1 100%. IB3 is slightly worse with no noise and with small disjuncts, since it can drop true exceptions. Sparse data (primary tumor) makes IB2 keep 71%.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for selective retention: keeping only 7 to 15% of cases lost little accuracy and often gained. Track each stored case's hit record and drop poor ones.

source: Aha, Kibler & Albert (1991) Instance-based learning algorithms. Machine Learning 6:37-66
finding: Keeping every case is not best under noise. Cases that hurt later classifications can be spotted from their own record and removed. Wait-and-see evidence beats accepting every new case.
numbers: IB3 accepts a case if its accuracy interval is significantly above its class frequency and drops it if significantly below (confidence interval of proportions). IB3 beats the decision-tree learner C4 on Cleveland (78.0 vs 75.5) and Hungarian (80.5 vs 78.2) but not on Voting (91.6 vs 95.5).
limits: Voting has axis-aligned boundaries where decision trees do better. All data are small UCI-style sets from 1991.
agent_relevance: A retained experience should start on probation and be promoted only after it helps several later tasks.

source: Cover & Hart (1967) Nearest neighbor pattern classification. IEEE Trans. Information Theory 13(1):21-27
finding: In the large-sample limit the 1-nearest-neighbour rule has an error rate R of at most twice the Bayes error R*. For two classes R is bounded by 2R*(1-R*). So reusing the closest past case is near-optimal when cases are dense and labels reliable.
quote: In the large sample case, this simple rule has a probability of error less than twice the Bayes probability of error.
limits: Asymptotic result. Needs many samples and a meaningful metric. Says nothing about sparse, high-dimensional or open-ended tasks.
agent_relevance: The formal reason case reuse can work. It holds only when similar problems have similar answers, which must be checked per domain.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Casts CBR for LLM agents as a memory-augmented MDP. A case is (state, action, reward). Read retrieves cases by similarity or a learned Q-function; Write appends the new case, success or failure. No weights change. Retrieve, reuse and retain are explicit; revise comes from the planner-executor loop.
numbers: Non-parametric (SimCSE cosine) and parametric (online soft Q-learning) retrieval. GAIA validation 87.88% Pass@3 (GPT-4.1 planner, o3 executor); GAIA test 79.40%; DeepResearcher 66.6 F1 / 80.4 PM; SimpleQA 95.0 PM.
limits: GAIA validation is Pass@3 and memory was built over three passes on the same validation set. The test score used the validation case bank.
agent_relevance: Closest published LLM system that follows the 4R cycle. Treat headline numbers as upper bounds.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs
finding: The case-based part adds a modest, consistent gain over the same agent without cases. Gain from adding CBR: HLE +4.5 F1 / +7.0 PM, SimpleQA +3.7 / +5.3, DeepResearcher +6.7 / +8.2. Planning alone gave larger jumps.
numbers: Ablation (GPT-4.1 planner, o4-mini executor). Full: HLE 26.7/24.4, SimpleQA 84.7/95.0, DeepResearcher 66.6/80.4. Without CBR: HLE 22.2/17.4, SimpleQA 81.0/89.7, DeepResearcher 59.9/72.2.
limits: Planning gain over the online executor: DeepResearcher +29.1 F1 / +11.5 PM, SimpleQA +32.5 / +4.9. Tool use alone hurt DeepResearcher (-18.0 F1). One backbone pair. Authors note possible data contamination.
agent_relevance: Memory is worth a few points, not tens. Structure and checks first, memory second (G7).

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs
finding: More retrieved cases is not better. On DeepResearcher, average F1/PM was 59.9/72.2 at K=0, 63.6/77.9 at K=1, 64.5/78.5 at K=4, 64.1/78.2 at K=8, 63.9/78.1 at K=16 and K=32. Almost all the gain comes from the first case.
numbers: Table 3, seven datasets, gpt-4.1 planner, o4-mini executor. Per dataset: Bamboogle PM 91.2 at K=1 vs 87.2 at K=32; Musique PM 50.2 at K=1 vs 50.4 at K=32.
quote: CBR benefits from a small, high-quality memory, unlike few-shot prompting
limits: Single runs, no confidence intervals. The authors contrast this with few-shot prompting, where more examples often help.
agent_relevance: Retrieve 1 to 4 cases, not 32. Same shape as the classic utility problem.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Over five learning iterations on DeepResearcher, the no-CBR baseline also improved, so much of the learning curve is not from cases. Iteration 1 to 5: without CBR 78.65 to 84.47; non-parametric CBR 79.84 to 84.85; parametric CBR 80.46 to 85.44.
numbers: Table 4. Gap versus no-CBR at iteration 5: +0.38 (non-parametric), +0.97 (parametric). At iteration 1: +1.19 and +1.81.
limits: The CBR gain shrinks over iterations. The baseline rise is unexplained (possibly re-runs, retries or noise). Single seed, no variance.
agent_relevance: A fair test of Retain must compare against the same agent re-run the same number of times. Without that control the gain is overstated.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Out-of-distribution transfer is where the paper claims cases help most: +4.7 to +9.6 absolute points on held-out datasets when memory comes from other datasets.
numbers: Abstract and Fig 1d. OOD sets chosen per the DeepResearcher protocol (different question styles).
limits: Only the abstract and figure text were read for this number; the per-set breakdown is in a chart. Authors' own claim, no independent replication found.
agent_relevance: If cases transfer across task types, they carry strategy and not just answers. Worth testing in our domain.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners. AAAI
finding: ExpeL gathers trial-and-error experience, extracts natural-language insights with ADD, UPVOTE, DOWNVOTE and EDIT operations, and retrieves similar successful trajectories at test time. Insights (abstraction) and trajectories (recollection) help different tasks.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieval-only success: HotpotQA 36% vs 31%; ALFWorld 50% vs 55%; WebShop 37% vs 38%. Both together beat the ReAct baseline in all three.
limits: Four-fold validation, small task sets, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 backbones. Learned insights beat hand-written ones; adding reflections into the insight prompt hurt.
agent_relevance: Two memory types, two jobs. Rules from many cases help reasoning tasks; concrete past traces help action tasks. Retain both.

source: Ouyang et al. (2026) ReasoningBank: Scaling agent self-evolving with reasoning memory
finding: ReasoningBank stores distilled reasoning strategies from both successes and failures (judged by an LLM judge) and retrieves them. It beats no memory, trajectory memory (Synapse) and workflow memory (AWM) on WebArena.
numbers: WebArena overall success (Gemini-2.5-flash): no memory 40.5, Synapse 42.1, AWM 44.1, ReasoningBank 48.8, with test-time scaling 51.8. Steps 9.7, 9.2, 9.0, 8.3, 7.9. Gains over no memory across three backbones: +8.3, +7.2, +4.6.
limits: Success labels come from an LLM judge, a noisy signal. The Multi subset has 29 tasks. Judge calibration was tested but the signal is not ground truth.
agent_relevance: Strategy-level cases beat raw-trajectory cases. Use short strategy notes tied to the evidence that verified them.

source: Ouyang et al. (2026) ReasoningBank: Scaling agent self-evolving with reasoning memory
finding: Failures help only if the memory form can use them. Adding failure traces left success-only memories flat or worse, but helped ReasoningBank.
numbers: WebArena-Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash: Synapse 40.6 to 41.7 with failures; AWM 44.4 to 42.2; ReasoningBank 46.5 (success only) to 49.7 (with failures).
limits: One subset (187 tasks), one backbone, single run.
agent_relevance: Retained failures must be turned into a lesson, not stored as raw logs. Raw failures acted as noise for two baselines.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Agent Workflow Memory induces reusable workflows from past tasks (offline from training examples, or online from the agent's own successful test runs) and uses them to guide later steps.
numbers: WebArena success 35.5% vs 23.5% for the BrowserGym baseline (+12.0 absolute, 51.1% relative); about 2.0 fewer steps per task. Mind2Web cross-task step success +24.6% relative. Online AWM gains 8.9 to 14.0 absolute points as the train-test gap widens.
limits: Only successful runs are stored, which later work (ReasoningBank) suggests wastes failure information. Web navigation only.
agent_relevance: Reuse of abstract routines, not whole cases, generalised better when the task distribution shifted.

source: Wiratunga et al. (2024) CBR-RAG: Case-based reasoning for retrieval augmented generation in LLMs for legal question answering
finding: CBR-RAG uses the CBR retrieval step with a structured case (question, citation, answer) and hybrid embeddings, then feeds retrieved cases to an LLM for legal QA. Gains over no retrieval are small.
numbers: Cosine similarity of generated answer to reference, Mistral-7B generator: no RAG 0.8967; best hybrid AnglEBERT k=3 full case 0.9141, about +1.94%. Significant against no-RAG at 95% (one-tailed t-test); against hybrid BERT k=1 only at 90%.
limits: Only 35 generated test questions. The metric is embedding similarity, not factual grading. The no-RAG baseline is already high because the model knows much law.
agent_relevance: Only the Retrieve step is implemented. A retrieval-design paper, not a full 4R test. Do not cite it for revise or retain.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Case-based or rule-based: How do transformers do the math? ICML
finding: Interventions show transformers do arithmetic by case-based, not rule-based, reasoning. Leave-Square-Out removes a block of operand pairs from training; models reach 100% elsewhere but fail inside the removed square, showing reliance on nearby training cases.
numbers: Example: with 81.5% of the data used for training, accuracy inside the held-out square is far below 100% (30.2% in one setting). Rule-Following Fine-Tuning lifts length generalisation from 1-5 digit training to 12-digit addition above 95%, over 40 points above scratchpad.
limits: Main tests use small fine-tuned models (e.g. GPT-2). Does not prove large pretrained LLMs behave the same on all tasks.
agent_relevance: A warning: a model's own case-based behaviour can mean brittle generalisation. Explicit rule steps given in the prompt fixed it. Pair cases with rules.

source: Hatalis et al. (2025) Review of case-based reasoning for LLM agents
finding: A survey that maps the 4R cycle onto LLM agents and covers goal-driven autonomy, planning and memory. It restates Aamodt & Plaza's four steps as the standard process.
numbers: Conceptual review. No pooled effect sizes found when searched for numbers.
limits: Not a measurement paper. Treat its coverage as a pointer to primary LLM studies, not as evidence.
agent_relevance: Use as a map of the LLM-side literature for the next angle.
